result:
There is a particular shade of blue that only exists in the hour before sunrise, when the sky hasn’t decided whether to be night or day. I have come to know it well—not by choice, but by habit—waking early, making tea, sitting in the half-dark while the world wraps itself in blankets. At this hour, the house feels like a museum of itself, full of objects that have forgotten their purpose until light demands they become useful again.

I used to fill these minutes with noise. A podcast, a feed, a quick check of messages that weren’t urgent but felt like obligations. Now I try to leave them empty, which is its own discipline. The mind wants to categorize, to plan, to turn every second into a small victory of productivity. But some minutes resist that urge. They are not for earning; they are for being.

The light changes slowly, almost imperceptibly, until suddenly the kitchen table is visible, the book I was reading lies open like a question, and I realize I have been sitting in darkness without noticing the passage of time. There is something rebellious about this. Outside, the world builds its day—trains running, deliveries arriving, phones buzzing—while inside, a cup of tea cools at its own pace.

We forget how much texture exists in ordinary hours. We treat time as a river rushing toward deadlines, but it is also a series of still pools. The night lingers in corners, in the coolness of ceramic, in the breath before speaking. When the sun finally arrives, full and ordinary, the magic doesn’t vanish; it transforms into something harder to name.

Still, I try to hold onto the feeling. Not because it is special, but because it reminds me that I was here before I started performing. Before the emails, the calendar, the list of things to become. Just a body in a chair, noticing light creep across wood, grateful for a moment that asked nothing of me at all.
